references.text: The context for Jesus' meeting with Zacchaeus: Zacchaeus had climbed up into a sycamore-fig tree to see Jesus ([ref:Luk 19:1-4|Luke 19:1-4]). Jesus stopped right at this tree and called him down.
Zacchaeus' response to Jesus' words – he quickly came down and welcomed Jesus with joy, while the crowd grumbled that Jesus had gone in to be a guest of a sinful man ([ref:Luk 19:6-7|Luke 19:6-7]).
Jesus explains the purpose of his visit to Zacchaeus: "For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" ([ref:Luk 19:10|Luke 19:10]). This shows why Jesus "had to" stay at Zacchaeus' house.

Jesus takes the initiative to enter people's homes and lives: "See, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him" ([ref:Åp 3:20|Revelation 3:20]). The same pattern as with Zacchaeus – Jesus invites himself in.
The parable of the lost sheep shows that Jesus actively seeks out those who are gone astray ([ref:Luk 15:4-6|Luke 15:4-6]). In this way, he also seeks out Zacchaeus directly and personally.

Jesus demonstrates supernatural knowledge about people he meets, just as he knew Nathanael's name and character ([ref:Joh 1:47-48|John 1:47-48]). Similarly, Jesus called Zacchaeus by name even though they had never met before.

Jesus went in and ate with tax collectors and sinners at Levi/Matthew's house, defending this by saying that it is the sick who need a doctor ([ref:Luk 5:29-32|Luke 5:29-32]). Jesus shows the same pattern with Zacchaeus, another chief tax collector.
Jesus was called "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" ([ref:Luk 7:34|Luke 7:34]). The visit to Zacchaeus illustrates this reputation concretely.

"He had to go through Samaria" ([ref:Joh 4:4|John 4:4]) – the divine "had to" (δεῖ) is also used in Luke 19:5 ("δεῖ με μεῖναι"). In both places, this points to God's plan of salvation that drives Jesus' actions.
Even as a twelve-year-old, Jesus used the divine "δεῖ" – he "had to" be in his Father's house ([ref:Luk 2:49|Luke 2:49]). The same word of necessity is used regarding the stay at Zacchaeus' home.
The Son of Man has not come to destroy people's lives, but to save them ([ref:Luk 9:56|Luke 9:56]). Jesus' visit to Zacchaeus is a concrete expression of this saving work.
The Lord himself will seek out his sheep and care for them ([ref:Esek 34:11-12|Ezekiel 34:11-12]). Jesus fulfills this prophecy by actively seeking out Zacchaeus, the lost one.
